notes: Source TTM ROCE repeated TTM ROE; showing FY26 ROCE instead.

debt_to_assets.label: Debt / assets
debt_to_assets.what: Debt (or all liabilities) as a share of total assets. The equity ratio is the opposite: equity as a share of assets.
debt_to_assets.read: Rising ratios over several years mean the company is relying more on outside money.
debt_to_assets.why: They show how much of what the company owns is funded by others.
debt_to_assets.formula: Total borrowings ÷ total assets, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

rota.label: Return on tangible assets
rota.what: Net profit as a share of physical and financial assets, leaving out goodwill and other intangibles.
rota.read: Use it alongside ROA when a company has bought many businesses.
rota.why: It removes the effect of past acquisitions, which inflate assets with goodwill.
rota.formula: The provider's net profit ÷ tangible assets (total assets less goodwill and other intangibles).

roa.label: ROA
roa.what: Net profit earned for every ₹100 of assets the company owns.
roa.read: For banks, an ROA above about 1% is generally considered good.
roa.why: It is especially useful for banks and other lenders, whose assets are mostly loans.
roa.formula: Net profit ÷ total assets at the year end.
roa.note: FinLit divides net profit by total assets at the year end.

quick_ratio.label: Quick ratio
quick_ratio.what: Like the current ratio but leaving out inventory, which may be slow to sell.
quick_ratio.read: A quick ratio near or above 1 means short-term bills are covered without selling stock.
quick_ratio.why: It is a stricter test of whether bills can be paid quickly.
quick_ratio.formula: (Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

cash_conversion_cycle.label: Cash conversion cycle
cash_conversion_cycle.what: The number of days between paying for materials and collecting cash from customers.
cash_conversion_cycle.read: A cycle that lengthens year after year signals tightening cash.
cash_conversion_cycle.why: A short or negative cycle means suppliers effectively fund the business.
cash_conversion_cycle.formula: Inventory days + debtor days − payable days, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

dividend_payout.label: Dividend payout
dividend_payout.what: The share of profit paid out as dividends.
dividend_payout.read: Above 100% means the company is paying more than it earns, which cannot last.
dividend_payout.why: Low payout keeps cash for growth; high payout returns more now but leaves less to reinvest.
dividend_payout.formula: Dividend per share declared for the year ÷ EPS of the same year; blank when EPS is not positive.

debt_to_fcf.label: Debt / free cash flow
debt_to_fcf.what: Total debt divided by yearly free cash flow: how many years of spare cash it would take to repay all debt.
debt_to_fcf.read: Lower is better; a falling figure over years means the company is de-risking.
debt_to_fcf.why: It tests whether debt is affordable from real cash, not accounting profit.
debt_to_fcf.formula: Total borrowings ÷ free cash flow of the year, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

lt_debt_to_equity.label: Long-term debt / equity
lt_debt_to_equity.what: Only borrowings due after more than a year, divided by equity.
lt_debt_to_equity.read: A sharp rise usually means a big expansion or acquisition is being funded with loans.
lt_debt_to_equity.why: Long-term debt funds factories and projects; short-term debt funds daily operations.
lt_debt_to_equity.formula: Borrowings due after more than a year ÷ shareholders' equity, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

financial_leverage.label: Financial leverage
financial_leverage.what: Total assets divided by shareholders' equity.
financial_leverage.read: A value of 2.4 means owners fund about 42% of assets and liabilities fund the rest.
financial_leverage.why: It shows how much of the asset base is funded by owners versus others.
financial_leverage.formula: Total assets ÷ shareholders' equity, as sent by the provider. Blank when equity is zero or negative.

asset_turnover.label: Asset turnover
asset_turnover.what: Revenue divided by average total assets: how many rupees of sales each rupee of assets produces.
asset_turnover.read: Retailers have high asset turnover; power companies have low. Compare within an industry.
asset_turnover.why: High turnover means assets are used intensively.
asset_turnover.formula: The provider's asset turnover. Where it sends none, FinLit uses revenue ÷ total assets at the year end (not the average of two years). Not shown for banks and lenders.
asset_turnover.note: FinLit uses the provider's figure, or revenue ÷ year-end total assets when none is sent; not the average of two years.

roce.label: ROCE
roce.what: Operating profit (EBIT) earned for every ₹100 of total capital used in the business, from both shareholders and lenders.
roce.read: A ROCE consistently above the cost of borrowing (roughly 10–12% in India) suggests the business creates value.
roce.why: Unlike ROE, it cannot be boosted by borrowing, so it is a fairer test of the business itself.
roce.formula: The provider's return on capital. Where the provider sends none, FinLit works out EBIT ÷ (total assets − current liabilities), with EBIT = profit before tax + finance costs. Not shown for banks and lenders.
roce.note: FinLit shows the provider's return on capital. Where none is sent, FinLit uses EBIT ÷ (total assets − current liabilities), not equity plus debt as above.

interest_coverage.label: Interest coverage
interest_coverage.what: Operating profit (EBIT) divided by interest expense: how many times over the company can pay its interest.
interest_coverage.read: Below 1.5 is weak, above 3 is generally comfortable; FinLit flags 'weak interest cover' as a red flag.
interest_coverage.why: Low coverage means a small fall in profit could make interest hard to pay.
interest_coverage.formula: EBIT ÷ interest expense, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

inventory_days.label: Inventory days
inventory_days.what: How many days, on average, goods sit in stock before being sold.
inventory_days.read: Rising inventory days can be an early sign of slowing demand.
inventory_days.why: Fewer days means less cash tied up and less risk of stock going obsolete.
inventory_days.formula: Inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × 365, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

retention_ratio.label: Retention ratio
retention_ratio.what: The share of profit kept in the business rather than paid out.
retention_ratio.read: Retention only helps owners if the company earns a good return (ROE) on what it keeps.
retention_ratio.formula: Share of profit kept in the business, as sent by the provider (100% − payout).

debtor_days.label: Debtor days
debtor_days.what: How many days, on average, customers take to pay.
debtor_days.read: Compare with peers and with the company's own trend.
debtor_days.why: Slow collection ties up cash and can hide weak sales quality.
debtor_days.formula: Receivables ÷ revenue × 365, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

current_ratio.label: Current ratio
current_ratio.what: Current assets divided by current liabilities: can the company pay bills due within a year from assets it will turn into cash within a year?
current_ratio.read: Around 1.2 to 2 is typical; well below 1 can mean a cash squeeze, though some businesses run safely that way.
current_ratio.why: It is a basic test of short-term safety.
current_ratio.formula: Current assets ÷ current liabilities, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

net_margin.label: Net margin
net_margin.what: The share of revenue that ends up as net profit after every cost and tax.
net_margin.read: A net margin of 7.5% means ₹7.50 of profit for every ₹100 of sales.
net_margin.why: It shows how much of each ₹100 of sales the shareholders keep.
net_margin.formula: Net profit ÷ total income (sales plus other income), as measured by the provider.
net_margin.note: The provider's margins are measured against total income (sales plus other income); the statements net margin used by the score and screener divides by sales.

effective_tax_rate.label: Effective tax rate
effective_tax_rate.what: The tax a company actually paid as a share of its profit before tax.
effective_tax_rate.read: Indian companies usually pay about 25%; ask why if the rate is far from that.
effective_tax_rate.why: An unusually low rate in one year can flatter profit and make growth from that year look slow later.
effective_tax_rate.formula: Tax expense ÷ profit before tax; blank when profit before tax is not positive.

payable_days.label: Payable days
payable_days.what: How many days, on average, the company takes to pay its suppliers.
payable_days.read: Very long payable days can mean the company is short of cash.
payable_days.why: Paying later keeps cash in the business longer.
payable_days.formula: Payables ÷ cost of goods sold × 365, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

roe.label: ROE
roe.what: How much profit a company makes for every ₹100 its shareholders have put in and left in the business.
roe.read: Compare with peers and the company's own past. Check debt too: borrowing can push ROE up.
roe.why: It shows whether owners' money is being used well; a business that earns more on each rupee can grow without asking for more.
roe.formula: The provider's return on equity: net profit ÷ shareholders' equity at the year end (not the average of two years). Blank when equity is zero or negative.
roe.note: FinLit shows the data provider's ROE: net profit ÷ shareholders' equity at the year end, not the average of two years.

pretax_margin.label: Pre-tax margin
pretax_margin.what: Profit before tax as a share of revenue.
pretax_margin.read: If pre-tax margin rises while operating margin falls, other income or lower interest is doing the work.
pretax_margin.why: It includes interest and other income, so it shows the full picture before tax.
pretax_margin.formula: Profit before tax ÷ total income (sales plus other income), as measured by the provider.

debt_to_equity.label: Debt / equity
debt_to_equity.what: Total borrowings divided by shareholders' equity: how much the company has borrowed for every rupee owners have put in. Some sources use total liabilities instead of borrowings.
debt_to_equity.read: Below 0.5 is generally comfortable for non-financial companies; banks are always much higher and need different measures.
debt_to_equity.why: More debt means fixed interest costs that must be paid even in bad years.
debt_to_equity.formula: Total borrowings ÷ shareholders' equity, as sent by the provider. Borrowings are loans, bonds and debentures (an NBFC's deposits count too). Blank when equity is zero or negative. Not shown for banks and lenders.
debt_to_equity.note: FinLit uses borrowings (loans, bonds, debentures; an NBFC's deposits count too) over shareholders' equity.

ebitda_margin.label: EBITDA margin
ebitda_margin.what: EBITDA as a share of revenue.
ebitda_margin.read: Look for stable or rising EBITDA margins through good and bad years.
ebitda_margin.why: A common way to compare operating strength across companies in the same industry.
ebitda_margin.formula: The provider's EBITDA ÷ total income (sales plus other income). Not shown for banks and lenders.

gross_margin.label: Gross margin
gross_margin.what: The share of revenue left after the direct cost of making the product or delivering the service.
gross_margin.read: Compare within an industry: a software firm's gross margin will always beat a steel maker's.
gross_margin.why: High gross margins suggest pricing power or a valuable brand.
gross_margin.formula: (Revenue − cost of goods sold) ÷ revenue, as sent by the data provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

ebit_margin.label: EBIT margin
ebit_margin.what: EBIT is Earnings Before Interest and Tax: profit after depreciation but before interest and tax. EBIT margin is EBIT as a share of revenue.
ebit_margin.read: Use EBIT to judge capital-heavy businesses such as telecom, cement or power.
ebit_margin.why: EBIT counts the cost of using up equipment, so it is a stricter measure than EBITDA.
ebit_margin.formula: The provider's EBIT ÷ total income (sales plus other income). Not shown for banks and lenders.

operating_margin.label: Operating margin
operating_margin.what: The share of income left after operating costs and depreciation, before interest and tax, measured against total income (sales plus other income).
operating_margin.read: A margin rising steadily over several years usually means growing efficiency or pricing power.
operating_margin.why: It shows how efficiently the core business runs.
operating_margin.formula: The provider's operating margin: (operating profit − depreciation + other income) ÷ total income. This is not the same line as 'Operating margin (statements)', which divides operating profit by sales alone.
operating_margin.note: FinLit has two operating margins: the provider's (operating profit − depreciation + other income, over total income) and the statements one (operating profit ÷ sales), which the score and screener use.

revenue_cagr_3y.label: 3Y sales CAGR
revenue_cagr_3y.what: Average yearly growth in sales over the last 3 years.
revenue_cagr_3y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
revenue_cagr_3y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
revenue_cagr_3y.formula: (Sales this year ÷ sales 3 years ago)^(1 ÷ 3) − 1, on the Revenue line of FinLit's P&L (a lender: interest earned).
revenue_cagr_3y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

revenue_cagr_5y.label: 5Y sales CAGR
revenue_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in sales over the last 5 years.
revenue_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
revenue_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
revenue_cagr_5y.formula: (Sales this year ÷ sales 5 years ago)^(1 ÷ 5) − 1, on the Revenue line of FinLit's P&L (a lender: interest earned).
revenue_cagr_5y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

profit_cagr_3y.label: 3Y profit CAGR
profit_cagr_3y.what: Average yearly growth in net profit over the last 3 years.
profit_cagr_3y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
profit_cagr_3y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
profit_cagr_3y.formula: The provider's 3-year compound growth in net profit.
profit_cagr_3y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

profit_cagr_5y.label: 5Y profit CAGR
profit_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in net profit over the last 5 years.
profit_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
profit_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
profit_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in net profit.
profit_cagr_5y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

eps_cagr_5y.label: 5Y EPS CAGR
eps_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in earnings per share over the last 5 years.
eps_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
eps_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
eps_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in earnings per share.
eps_cagr_5y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

ebitda_cagr_5y.label: 5Y EBITDA CAGR
ebitda_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in EBITDA over the last 5 years.
ebitda_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
ebitda_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
ebitda_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in EBITDA.
ebitda_cagr_5y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

book_value_cagr_5y.label: 5Y book value CAGR
book_value_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in book value over the last 5 years.
book_value_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
book_value_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
book_value_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in book value (shareholders' equity).
book_value_cagr_5y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

cfo_cagr_3y.label: 3Y operating cash CAGR
cfo_cagr_3y.what: Average yearly growth in operating cash flow over the last 3 years.
cfo_cagr_3y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
cfo_cagr_3y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
cfo_cagr_3y.formula: The provider's 3-year compound growth in operating cash flow.
cfo_cagr_3y.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

opm.label: Operating margin (statements)
opm.what: The share of revenue left after operating costs, before interest and tax.
opm.read: A margin rising steadily over several years usually means growing efficiency or pricing power.
opm.why: It shows how efficiently the core business runs.
opm.formula: Operating profit ÷ sales for the latest full year, from FinLit's own P&L (a lender: ÷ total income). Operating profit is before depreciation, interest and other income.
opm.note: FinLit has two operating margins: the provider's (operating profit − depreciation + other income, over total income) and the statements one (operating profit ÷ sales), which the score and screener use.

npm.label: Net margin (statements)
npm.what: The share of revenue that ends up as net profit after every cost and tax.
npm.read: A net margin of 7.5% means ₹7.50 of profit for every ₹100 of sales.
npm.why: It shows how much of each ₹100 of sales the shareholders keep.
npm.formula: Net profit ÷ sales for the latest full year, from FinLit's own P&L (a lender: ÷ total income). Net profit is the part that belongs to the company's shareholders.
npm.note: The provider's margins are measured against total income (sales plus other income); the statements net margin used by the score and screener divides by sales.

liabilities_to_assets.label: Liabilities / assets
liabilities_to_assets.what: Debt (or all liabilities) as a share of total assets. The equity ratio is the opposite: equity as a share of assets.
liabilities_to_assets.read: Rising ratios over several years mean the company is relying more on outside money.
liabilities_to_assets.why: They show how much of what the company owns is funded by others.
liabilities_to_assets.formula: Total liabilities ÷ total assets on the latest annual balance sheet. Not shown for banks and lenders.

sales_growth_latest.label: Sales growth (latest year)
sales_growth_latest.what: Growth in sales over the latest year.
sales_growth_latest.read: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
sales_growth_latest.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
sales_growth_latest.formula: Sales this year ÷ sales last year − 1. For a company with only one annual result, the latest quarter against the same quarter a year earlier (the shown period says so).

profit_growth_latest.label: Profit growth (latest year)
profit_growth_latest.what: Growth in net profit over the latest year.
profit_growth_latest.read: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
profit_growth_latest.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
profit_growth_latest.formula: Net profit this year ÷ net profit last year − 1; blank when last year's profit was zero or a loss. For a company with only one annual result, the latest quarter against the same quarter a year earlier.

market_cap.label: Market cap
market_cap.what: The total market value of a company: share price multiplied by the number of shares.
market_cap.read: ₹16 lakh crore market cap means the market values the whole company at that amount today.
market_cap.why: It tells you how big the company is in the stock market's eyes and decides whether it is a large, mid or small cap.
market_cap.formula: Share price × shares outstanding, in ₹ crore, as sent with the latest quote.

dividend_yield.label: Dividend yield
dividend_yield.what: Yearly dividend per share as a percentage of the current share price.
dividend_yield.read: A 0.5% yield means ₹0.50 a year per ₹100 invested. Very high yields can signal that the market expects a cut.
dividend_yield.why: It tells you the cash income you get for each ₹100 invested at today's price.
dividend_yield.formula: Dividends per share with an ex-date in the last 12 months ÷ the latest price.

cfo_to_pat.label: Cash conversion (CFO/PAT)
cfo_to_pat.what: Operating cash flow as a percentage of net profit. FinLit also shows free cash flow to profit.
cfo_to_pat.read: Around 80% or more over several years is healthy; FinLit flags 'profit not backed by cash' when it is weak.
cfo_to_pat.why: It tests whether reported profit is turning into real cash.
cfo_to_pat.formula: Operating cash flow ÷ net profit for the latest year that has both, as a percentage. Left blank when profit is zero or negative. Not shown for banks and lenders.

fcf_to_pat.label: FCF / PAT
fcf_to_pat.what: Free cash flow as a percentage of net profit: how much of the profit is left as spare cash after capital spending.
fcf_to_pat.read: Around 80% or more over several years is healthy; FinLit flags 'profit not backed by cash' when it is weak.
fcf_to_pat.why: It tests whether reported profit is turning into real cash.
fcf_to_pat.formula: Free cash flow ÷ net profit for the latest year that has both, as a percentage. Left blank when profit is zero or negative. Not shown for banks and lenders.

sales_cagr.label: Sales CAGR
sales_cagr.what: Average yearly growth in sales (up to 5 years).
sales_cagr.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
sales_cagr.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
sales_cagr.formula: (Sales this year ÷ sales N years ago)^(1 ÷ N) − 1 on FinLit's P&L, with N up to 5 years depending on how many years are held; the shown period says N.
sales_cagr.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

profit_cagr.label: Profit CAGR
profit_cagr.what: Average yearly growth in net profit (up to 5 years).
profit_cagr.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
profit_cagr.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
profit_cagr.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in net profit; where it sends none, FinLit works it out from its own P&L over up to 5 years. The shown period says how many.
profit_cagr.note: FinLit counts years by position in its yearly data and needs positive start and end values.

ev_ebitda.label: EV/EBITDA
ev_ebitda.read: Widely used for telecom, energy and industrial firms. Lower is cheaper, within the same industry.
ev_ebitda.why: It compares companies fairly regardless of how much debt they use.
ev_ebitda.formula: (Market cap + borrowings − cash and cash equivalents) ÷ trailing-twelve-month EBITDA from the provider; blank when EBITDA is not positive. Cash is the balance-sheet cash line only. Not shown for banks and lenders.

pe.label: P/E
pe.what: The share price divided by EPS: how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of yearly profit.
pe.read: Compare P/E with the company's own history and its industry. A low P/E can mean cheap, or it can mean the market expects profits to fall.
pe.why: It is the quickest way to judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its profits.
pe.formula: Share price ÷ earnings per share (trailing twelve months). The provider's figure, recalculated at the latest price; left blank when profit is zero or negative.
pe.note: FinLit recalculates the provider's P/E at the latest price and leaves it blank when profit is not positive.

pb.label: P/B
pb.what: The share price divided by book value per share: what you pay for each rupee of net assets.
pb.read: A P/B below 1 means the market values the company below its book value; find out why before calling it cheap.
pb.why: Most useful for banks, insurers and asset-heavy companies, whose assets are close to their real value.
pb.formula: Share price ÷ book value per share. The provider's figure, recalculated at the latest price; left blank when equity is zero or negative.

ps.label: P/S
ps.what: Market cap divided by yearly revenue.
ps.read: Compare only within an industry; high-margin businesses naturally trade at higher P/S.
ps.why: Useful for young or loss-making companies that have no profit to put in a P/E.
ps.formula: Market cap ÷ yearly sales. The provider's figure, recalculated at the latest price.

pfcf.label: P/FCF
pfcf.what: Market cap divided by yearly operating cash flow (P/CFO) or by free cash flow (P/FCF).
pfcf.read: If P/FCF is far higher than P/E, profits are not turning into spare cash.
pfcf.why: Cash is harder to dress up than profit, so these ratios can be more reliable than P/E.
pfcf.formula: Market cap ÷ free cash flow. The provider's figure, recalculated at the latest price; left blank when free cash flow is not positive. Not shown for banks and lenders.
